svg.title: What redistribution actually loses, the seed metric problem, and the two-point feedback loop
svg.desc: Left panel shows two domains joined by a boundary router. Three things are lost at the boundary: the metric, because costs are not comparable across protocols and the seed value must be supplied explicitly; the path reasoning, because the receiving protocol sees only a static-like prefix with no history; and the failure knowledge, because the boundary router decides the whole domain's reachability. A note explains that a missing seed metric produces either a zero cost that wins every comparison or infinity that never installs, and both failures are silent. Right panel shows two boundary routers redistributing in both directions, forming a feedback loop: each learns the other's redistributed copy, the metric worsens on each pass, and the loop only stops when both directions are filtered or tagged. The recommended pattern is shown: tag redistributed routes with a well-known value, then deny that tag on the way back in.
svg.text: Redistribution is not a translation; it is a lossy conversion with a seed value
Every problem it causes comes from one of three losses, and all three are silent until traffic stops
THE BOUNDARY
OSPF domain
ASBR
redistribute
EIGRP domain
Loss 1 — the metric. Cost 20 and metric 2 816 000 are not comparable, so a seed
must be supplied by hand. Omit it and you get 0 (wins everything) or infinity (never installs).
Loss 2 — the reasoning. The receiver sees a prefix with no history, only a claim.
Loss 3 — the failure knowledge. The boundary decides reachability for the whole domain.
THE TWO-POINT FEEDBACK LOOP
R1
R2
R1 → OSPF → R2
R2 → OSPF → R1 · metric worsens each pass
Both routers redistribute in both directions, so each
relearns the other's copy of the same prefix. The loop
stops only when one direction is filtered or tagged.
A flapping link then makes the metric climb indefinitely.
THE PATTERN THAT WORKS
Step 1 · tag on the way out
route-map SET-TAG permit 10
set tag 100
Step 2 · deny the tag coming in
route-map INTO-EIGRP deny 5
match tag 100
Step 3 · explicit seed metric
redistribute ospf 1 metric 100000
Step 4 · one-way is the default
Prefer a single boundary. Two-way at two points
costs more than the redundancy is worth.
Why this is the fourth-quarter outage: redistribution is configured once, works, and is never tested again. Then someone adds a
summary, or a second boundary, or a static route for a migration — and the loop or the zero seed metric that was there all along becomes
visible. The design document must state, for every boundary: direction, seed metric, tag, and which prefixes are allowed through, both ways.
If that table cannot be filled in, the boundary is not designed — it is merely configured.

Test in every change window: add the new prefix on the far side, then confirm from both domains that exactly one path exists and that its metric is the intended one. Repeat with the boundary link down.
